Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not clearly linked to the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery, and no other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal item provides a plausible religious cue or meaning that would explain this highly specific avoidance.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized hypervigilance after robbery, but specifically listening for someone entering the home implies a home-intrusion context that is unsupported by the trauma type and by the rest of the selected items; this makes the item hard to reconcile with the same indexed event.

vignette: Six months prior, Nour, a twenty-six-year-old non-binary Middle Eastern American veterinarian, was walking home after a long shift when a stranger stepped from a narrow, windowless alley, pressing a knife against their ribs and demanding a wallet and phone. The robbery was defined by the cold bite of steel, the attacker’s ragged breathing, and the sudden, suffocating certainty that Nour would not survive the encounter. In the weeks that followed, the experience shattered their previous sense of stability, quickly crystallizing into the negative appraisal that they had lost their happiness and could not rely on other people for safety. Because this conviction took hold, Nour’s nervous system defaulted to constant vigilance, causing them to continuously scan for danger in every clinic corridor and feel perpetually on guard even inside their own apartment. The hypervigilance was so absolute that Nour found themselves frequently checking behind clients during consultations and constantly checking behind themselves in familiar neighborhoods, as if the threat were still actively pursuing them. The belief that the world remained fundamentally unpredictable left the traumatic fragments entirely unprocessed, which meant that ordinary sensory cues would instantly trigger the full memory without warning. During a routine examination of an anxious German Shepherd in the clinic’s sterile exam room, the overlapping antiseptic and stale tobacco scents morphed into the exact olfactory recall of the alley, and the vivid reconstruction of the knife against their ribs flooded their system. When those unbidden memories surfaced, the mind misinterpreted the recollection as an immediate present danger, triggering another round of scanning for danger and compulsively checking behind the treatment table. The inability to explain clearly what had happened only compounded the intrusion; when Nour tried to recount the robbery to their partner, they would lose the thread and stop mid-sentence, leaving the unprocessed fragments to fester. This lack of narrative control reinforced the negative appraisal that happiness was permanently gone, because the mind could not reconcile the past with a safe present, locking Nour into the conviction that they must be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. As the traumatic recall grew more frequent, the defensive strategies emerged as the only available escape. When the phantom scent hit during quiet evenings, Nour would retreat into magical thinking, insisting to themselves that the event did not really happen or was not that bad, while simultaneously adopting a fawning response whenever their partner raised their voice, hoping overly compliance might ward off imagined threats. The sheer exhaustion of monitoring for danger made leaving the house feel impossible, so Nour began avoiding going out altogether. Because Nour remained so tightly wound and alert to every shadow, the nervous system stayed primed to latch onto environmental cues, which in turn made the memories erupt with even greater intensity. By sealing themselves inside and refusing to process the event through normal engagement, the avoidance only ensured that the unprocessed fragments continued to surface, often triggered without warning in the stillness of the empty clinic. The clinical picture tightened as the habits solidified. The fawning responses in professional settings drove clients away and strained Nour’s relationship, which only validated the negative appraisal that they could not rely on others and that joy was permanently inaccessible. As the magical thinking failed to quiet the alarm bells, the refusal to go out merely trapped Nour in a sensory-deprived loop, causing the internal threat system to fire constantly and sustaining the relentless scanning and checking behind every doorway. Now, sitting in the sterile waiting area of a trauma clinic, Nour finally reached out for professional support, terrified that the self-reinforcing loop of fear was irreversible, yet desperately hoping to reclaim the ability to walk down the street without bracing for a blade or dissolving into unexplainable panic.
